(There, seif 3) A stolen sukkah is valid, etc. Note: The Magen Avraham brought in this siman the view of Sefer Yere'im, that theft from a gentile, even if permitted, is nevertheless not called "yours"; see there. I have a very great astonishment about his words from the Talmud in Sotah 43b, where it asks regarding what we say, "he dedicated it and did not inaugurate it" excludes a robber: let us say this is not like R. Yose HaGelili, who says that "the fearful and fainthearted" means one who is afraid because of transgressions in his hand. It answers: even if you say it is R. Yose HaGelili, it is where he repented and paid money. If so, he should have bought it and then returned, since from the outset it came into his hand as theft. End quote of the Talmud. This is difficult: what forced it to answer this? It would have been better to answer that it speaks of theft from a gentile; if so there is no transgression, and nevertheless it is not his and is not called "he inaugurated it," and therefore he does not return. R. Yose could hold like the one who says theft from a gentile is permitted, and the one who says theft from a gentile is forbidden could hold like the rabbis, who do not accept "one who is afraid because of transgressions in his hand." It would then accord with everyone either way. Perforce it is proven that if theft from a gentile is permitted, it is truly his, it is his house, and it is like an actual purchase. Why should he not return? This is proof against the author of Yere'im, and it requires great examination. Examine carefully. While on this subject, another difficulty arose for me from the Talmud in Sukkah 33, where we say that one fulfills with a sukkah on stolen land because it holds that land is not stolen, and it is considered a borrowed sukkah. This is difficult: since we rule that a mitzvah that comes through a transgression is invalid, either way there is a problem. If with stolen land there is the prohibition of "you shall not steal," then it is a mitzvah that comes through a transgression, so why does one fulfill with a stolen sukkah? And if with land, since it is not stolen, there is no prohibition of "you shall not steal," then what does the Talmud ask in Sotah, to say it is not like R. Yose HaGelili, who says "one who is afraid because of transgressions in his hand"? One can say it accords even with R. Yose HaGelili and speaks of stolen land, where there is no prohibition of "you shall not steal." See what the Magen Avraham wrote regarding a house, whether it can be stolen or not and whether its law is like land. This is difficult from here and requires great examination. Examine carefully. I have another difficulty against the above view of Sefer Yere'im, brought in Magen Avraham small paragraph 3, from the Talmud in Bava Kamma 113, which says there: Was it not taught that R. Shimon said, R. Akiva expounded this matter, etc.: From where do we know that theft from a gentile is forbidden? The verse says, "after he is sold, redemption shall be for him," that he should not seize him and leave; perhaps he may overcharge him? The verse says, "and he shall calculate with his buyer," he must be exact with his buyer, etc. This is difficult: from where do we know theft from him is forbidden? Perhaps it is always permitted, and the verse comes to say that since a Hebrew slave's body is acquired, as written there in the Gemara and in the first chapter of Kiddushin, then although theft from him is permitted, nevertheless since his body is acquired to him, his labor should belong to him and not be called "yours." If so, if he betroths a woman with it, she would not be betrothed; or if he buys an etrog or the like with it, he would not fulfill with it. This is what the Torah revealed, that he should not overcharge him, because otherwise it would not be called "yours." In my opinion this is a clear proof against Yere'im. Examine carefully. I have another strong difficulty against the above Yere'im from the Talmud at the beginning of the second chapter of Bechorot, 13b, where it says: according to the one who says theft from him is permitted, why do I need to exclude a gentile from the law of overcharging? According to the Yere'im's view, what is the question? Perhaps it teaches that with overcharging it is also called "yours." With theft, granted that it is permitted, nevertheless it is called theft and therefore is not "yours"; but from overcharging the Torah excludes him, so that it is not called overcharging at all, and therefore it is also "yours." Examine carefully, for this requires great examination. Now we learned in the first chapter of Sukkah: that phrase is needed to exclude a stolen sukkah. Tosafot wrote: This is puzzling; let it follow because it is a mitzvah that comes through a transgression, etc. However, there one can answer that it was needed to exclude a borrowed one; but regarding sukkah one cannot answer this according to the rabbis, who say below in chapter HaYashen that a person fulfills his obligation with his fellow's sukkah, and they derive it from "all the native-born in Israel shall dwell in sukkot," teaching that all Israel are fit to sit in one sukkah, etc. Their language astonishes me: why did they need to lengthen and write "and they derive it," etc.? What practical difference is there for their question from where the rabbis learned it? In the end, we see that the rabbis hold a borrowed sukkah is valid. What appears to me, with God's help, is this. At first glance one might resolve their question, why do we need a verse to exclude a stolen one if it is a mitzvah that comes through a transgression, as follows: we rule that a person is pleased that a mitzvah be done with his property, so it would have been fitting to fulfill even with theft. But this is not so, for regarding the robber who harmed him, he is not pleased that a mitzvah be fulfilled with his property. Yet if so, this works for the robber, but for others who did not harm him, one can properly say that he is pleased for a mitzvah to be fulfilled with his property. Then there is no transgression, and therefore the Torah invalidated a stolen sukkah so that even others are invalid. But at first glance this is not so: if he is pleased for a mitzvah to be fulfilled with his property, then it is like borrowed, and a borrowed sukkah is valid. However, it works well. One can say that certainly, since it is written "for yourself," it implies that it is yours. With a borrowed sukkah, since he lends it to him knowingly, not only according to the one who says ownership of produce-rights is like ownership of the body is it certainly his with regard to the produce-rights; even according to the one who says it is not like ownership of the body, that applies only where ownership of the body is required, such as with first fruits, where one must say "the land that You gave me" and we require the body of the land to be his, so ownership of produce-rights is not like ownership of the body. But with sukkah, where the mitzvah is only sitting and we require only that the sitting be his, ownership of produce-rights is at least ownership with regard to the produce-rights, and it is called "for yourself." If so, since we at least require ownership of produce-rights, it is understandable where it is with his knowledge and he transfers it to him; but without his knowledge, it is ineffective, for transfer of ownership requires the owner's knowledge, and without his knowledge there is no transfer. But regarding theft of land, the matter depends only on objection; in that, without his knowledge works like with his knowledge. Therefore the verse "for yourself" was needed to exclude stolen, that even others do not fulfill. What is excluded as borrowed regarding lulav from "for yourselves" is because even borrowed is not "yours"; with lulav, which is only taking, there is no produce-benefit at all, and therefore even borrowed is not "yours," for with taking there is no benefit. But with sukkah, where the sitting is benefit and there is ownership of produce-rights, borrowed is included in "for yourself," while without his knowledge is not considered "for yourself." If so, their question would not be difficult. Therefore they introduced that the fact that borrowed is valid is learned from another verse, "the native-born." If it were true that borrowed is considered "for yourself" because of ownership of produce-rights and is unlike lulav, where there is no produce-benefit, why need another verse to validate borrowed? From the body of the verse "for yourself," borrowed should be valid. Since they learned it from another verse, it is proven that borrowed is not included in "for yourself" and is not considered his through ownership of the sitting; another verse was needed. If so, it is properly difficult: why do we need "for yourself"? Let it follow because it is a mitzvah that comes through a transgression. And one cannot say it is for others and because a person is pleased that a mitzvah be done with his property, for if so it is also not excluded by "for yourself," since it is borrowed; and since even borrowed is not called "for yourself," then there is no acquisition here, only his desire, and without his knowledge suffices. If so, it should also be valid despite theft. As for the robber himself, let it follow because it is a mitzvah that comes through a transgression. Therefore they needed to lengthen and state from where they learned this. This arose in my mind only as an observation. May our words be accepted before the Creator of the world and Dweller in heaven, amen. Examine carefully. Tosafot at the beginning of chapter Lulav HaGazul asked: why do we need the verse "for yourselves" to exclude a stolen one? Let it follow because it is a mitzvah that comes through a transgression. It appears that the practical difference is if gentiles coerced him to sit in his fellow's sukkah against his will. In this case, if the only reason were mitzvah through transgression, here there is no transgression because he was coerced; if in his heart he intended to fulfill the mitzvah of sukkah, he would fulfill. But if the Torah excluded a stolen sukkah as invalid, then although there is no transgression, in any event it is not his and not borrowed, and his intent is ineffective, since there is no act of sitting in a valid sukkah, as he is sitting in a stolen sukkah. One can also say that the practical difference is for a king, for it is stated in tractate Bava Kamma that theft does not apply to a king, since a king may break through a fence for himself to make a road, and no one protests. Nevertheless it appears that in any event it is not his; only there is no prohibition of "you shall not steal." Therefore in this case there is no transgression, but he nevertheless does not fulfill, since it is borrowed. Examine this. One can further answer Tosafot's question by saying the practical difference is if Levi stole from Reuven and Shimon from each one less than a perutah's worth and roofed with it. Although we rule that it is forbidden to steal even any amount, that is because a half-measure is Torah-forbidden, as the Sema wrote in Choshen Mishpat simanim 358 and 361. Nevertheless, one can say that a mitzvah that comes through a transgression applies only with a full measure and not with a half-measure, for the Shach wrote in Yoreh De'ah siman 238 that a half-measure is lighter even than a rabbinic prohibition and an oath takes effect upon it; so too it is explicit in Tosafot that an oath takes effect on a half-measure and it is not considered already sworn from Sinai. If so, one can say that even "already sworn" does not apply to less than the measure. Therefore, since from each person there is only less than a perutah, there is no mitzvah through transgression. But because of "for yourself" it is invalid: first, although it does not require return, in any event it is not yours and is not called "for yourself," and is worse than borrowed, for there it is with his knowledge and here without his knowledge. Further, in his possession there is a perutah's worth of theft, so in the end he is roofing with a perutah's worth of theft and does not fulfill his obligation with it. One can further say that the practical difference is if he stole roofing and roofed with it, and afterward bought it from the robber. It is then invalid because of theft, which is an intrinsic invalidity, and if so it is "make it, and not from what is already made," since it was made in invalidity, and its invalidity is like its body. See the Peri Megadim there, who was uncertain about this. In my humble opinion it appears so. But if its invalidity is because of a mitzvah that comes through a transgression, then we must say that the name of mitzvah takes effect upon it, for if there is no mitzvah in it, it has no invalidity except because it is a mitzvah. If so, the name of mitzvah must first take effect upon it, and then it is not relevant to invalidate it because of "make it and not from what is already made," for it cannot be invalidated without the mitzvah first taking effect. This is clear and correct. Examine carefully.
(There in the same seif, in the gloss) However, at the outset a person should not sit in his fellow's sukkah without his knowledge, all the more so if he intends to steal it; likewise, one should not at the outset make a sukkah on his fellow's land without his knowledge, etc. Note: We learned in the Talmud in Sukkah: The Rabbis taught: a stolen sukkah and one who roofs in the public domain, R. Eliezer invalidates and the sages validate. See there in the Talmud, where they disagree whether land is stolen or not. At first glance this is difficult for me: from where does R. Eliezer know that a sukkah in the public domain is invalid? Were it not that the verse revealed "for yourself" to exclude a stolen one, even an actually stolen sukkah would be valid; only the verse revealed "for yourself" to exclude stolen. If so, from where do we know that it is invalid even in the public domain? The Tosafot Yom Tov wrote in the first chapter of Orlah, Mishnah 2, regarding one who plants in the public domain, a gentile who planted, and a robber, etc., that it is liable in orlah. The Tosafot Yom Tov asked there that this is a case of "this, and it is unnecessary to say this": if one who plants in the public domain, where despair is not relevant, is liable, all the more so one who steals land and the owners despair. He answered as follows: one can say that since, in any event, land is not stolen, I might have thought he is more exempt than one who plants in the public domain, because an ordinary public domain has some connection to every person, to walk, stand, rest, and the like; therefore one who plants in it is liable because it is like one who plants in his own domain. This is unlike one who steals land, where even if the owners despaired, since despair does not apply to land, etc. He also brought there the words of the Rav of Bartenura, who holds that with stolen land he is liable only if the owner despaired, but if he did not despair he is exempt from orlah; see there. According to this, not only according to the Rav of Bartenura is it certainly proven that the public domain is better than theft from one's fellow, and the public domain is not considered so stolen, for in the public domain he is liable even without despair, since despair is not relevant, and nevertheless he is liable in orlah, whereas with theft from an individual he requires despair. Even according to the Tosafot Yom Tov, who holds that even without despair he is liable, it is also proven that the public domain is better, as the Tosafot Yom Tov himself wrote, for otherwise it would be difficult that this is a case of "this, and it is unnecessary to say this." If so, since the public domain is better than theft from an individual, and since with sukkah there is only one exclusion, "for yourself," excluding stolen, perhaps it excludes only theft from an individual, but in the public domain it is permitted, for the reason the Tosafot Yom Tov wrote: since each person has a share in it, it is like planting in one's own. From where do we know it is invalid in such a case? At first glance one could say that he derived this from Tosafot's question: why do we need "for yourself" to exclude stolen; let it follow because it is a mitzvah that comes through a transgression. It seems to me that in truth, with theft from an individual, no verse is needed, for it is a mitzvah that comes through a transgression. Therefore perforce this "for yourself," which excludes stolen, refers to the public domain, where there is no transgression because he too has a share in it; nevertheless it is not "for yourself," for it is not like borrowed, where the lender lends knowingly. But if he makes it in the public domain, in any event it is not with knowledge, so it is not borrowed. Nevertheless there is no transgression, and for this the verse "for yourself" excludes it. This works according to those who accept the principle of mitzvah through transgression. But what shall we do according to the one who does not hold of mitzvah through transgression at all, or according to the decisors who hold it is only rabbinic? Then the difficulty remains: perhaps "for yourself" excludes only a stolen sukkah from an individual and not the public domain. It appears that certainly the two depend on one another. According to R. Eliezer, who holds land is stolen, since he steals the body of the land, certainly the public domain is like theft from an individual, for the body of the land is not his and he is now stealing the land. On the contrary, the public domain is worse, for who can claim and who can forgive, as the Tosafot Yom Tov wrote in his question. Therefore certainly from this verse, "for yourself," both are excluded, for each has an advantage and a disadvantage and they are equal; which would you exclude? But the Mishnah in Orlah follows the rabbis, and according to us land is not stolen. If so, since wherever the body of the land is, it remains in the owner's domain, and he is not stealing the body of the land but only temporary use, and he has a share in the right to use it, the public domain is indeed better than an individual. Therefore the Mishnah in Orlah listed it in a way of "not only this, but even this." Examine carefully. What the Rema wrote, "and likewise a Jew should not cut the roofing, etc., but should buy it from a gentile": the language of Hagahot Ashiri in chapter 3 of Sukkah is as follows: Ra'avyah in the name of his father Rabbenu Yoel, that people must be careful not to cut willow for the lulav from the fields of a gentile, even with his permission, because ordinary gentiles are robbers of fields, etc. Rather, he should hire the gentile to cut it, so that owner-despair will be in their hand and change of domain in your hand. End quote. It implies that it is permitted to hire the gentile to cut. In truth this matter requires examination: from where do we know this is effective? The Talmud speaks where the gentile himself, the owner of the field, cuts it, and since it was his from the outset and he intends to steal it, the despair properly takes effect in their hand, and change of domain in yours. In that case, since he himself is the seller, he acts for his own intent and not for the Jew, and therefore the despair is in their hand. But if the Jew hires another gentile to cut, this gentile does not intend to steal it and does not do it for his own intent but only for the Jew. If so, the despair does not take effect in the gentile's hand, but only when it reaches the hand of the Jewish buyer who intends to acquire it; if so, it is still as though the Jew stole it. All the more so according to the Machaneh Ephraim in the laws of agency, who holds that where it is through hiring there is agency for a gentile, and this is brought in Sha'ar HaMelech, laws of Terumot; according to that it is even more difficult, for the gentile is the Jew's agent and it is as though the Jew stole it himself. One cannot say the intent of Hagahot Ashiri is that the same gentile who sells it to him hires himself out to cut, for if so why mention hiring? It is understandable if his intent is to another gentile, for he states the normal case, since a gentile would not obey him for free. One can also say that this itself teaches that even through hiring it is permitted for the gentile to cut. But if the intent is that same gentile himself, why mention hiring? Without hiring he will do so, for he needs to sell them, and if he does not cut, the Jew will not buy from him. He should have used the language of the Talmud: rather, let them cut it. Perforce his intent is another gentile, and if so it is difficult why this truly helps. The Rema indeed changed the language of Hagahot Ashiri and wrote only: he should buy from the gentile, etc. The words of Hagahot Ashiri require examination in this respect. Regarding the law whether it is permitted to make a sukkah in the public domain, I wrote to permit in Sefer HaChayim. Now I found a clear proof to this from the words of the Yerushalmi and the Rashba in his novellae to Bava Kamma at the end of chapter HaKones. This is his language there: R. Yochanan says that regarding a Chanukah lamp he is exempt because it is with permission, meaning with permission of mitzvah, as we say in chapter HaManiach Et HaKad regarding one who puts out his flax. However, not everyone who puts something out with permission of mitzvah is exempt, for if he made a mitzvah sukkah at the entrance of his house outside and people were damaged by it, he is liable, as stated in the Yerushalmi, such as those who make a sukkah at the entrance of their shops on the festival. But with Chanukah he is exempt, because there is a mitzvah to place it at the entrance of his house because of publicizing the miracle. End quote. His intent is clear: specifically with Chanukah, where it is specifically a mitzvah to place it outside, he is exempt. But with sukkah, since it is not specifically a mitzvah that it be outside, he is liable, even though in any event it is a valid sukkah and a mitzvah, for otherwise it is obvious he is liable. Perforce it is a valid sukkah. And what obligates him must be where he made it in the public domain, for if it were in his own domain he would be exempt for all damages. The main law of damages is where he did something in the public domain, as is proven in Bava Kamma in several places. Perforce it speaks where he made the sukkah in the public domain, and it is proven that it is a mitzvah and the sukkah is valid. This is clear and correct. I later remembered that this proof is already explained in Mekor Chayim from the Tosefta. In my Sefer HaChayim I rejected this; see there.

eliyah_rabbah.he: [ג] שלא מדעתו וכו'. והט"ז כתב שמותר ליכנס כמו בלולב עיין סימן תרמ"ט דניחא ליה לאינש למיעבד מצוה בממוניה ודוקא בשבעל סוכה אינו שם, אבל כשהוא שם מקפיד, עד כאן. ולעניות דעתי שאני לולב שאין צריך לו אלא לשעה מה שאין כן בסוכה מקפיד תמיד שיכסף ליכנס כשאחר שם דוגמא לזה בבבא מציעא דף כ"ב גבי כלך אצל יפות:
eliyah_rabbah.en: [3] Without his knowledge, etc. The Taz wrote that it is permitted to enter, as with lulav; see siman 649, because a person is pleased that a mitzvah be done with his property. This applies specifically when the owner of the sukkah is not there, but when he is there he objects. End quote. In my humble opinion, lulav is different, for one needs it only for a moment, unlike a sukkah, where he objects constantly, because he is embarrassed to enter when someone else is there. A similar case appears in Bava Metzia 22 regarding "go to the better ones."

levushei_serad.he: <small>סק"ה</small> בכל ענין רק רבנן עשו תקנה דסגי דדמי עצים וכיון דלא עביד תקנתא דרבנן נשאר בפסולי':
levushei_serad.en: SKA in every matter only a rabbi made a regulation of trees and trees, and since there was no worker, a rabbi remained in the wrong:

machatzit_hashekel.he:
(ס"ק ג) וכן כולי דהא בר"ה כו' עיין בח"מ סי' קס"ב סעיף ב' שכתב וז"ל וכן מבואות המפולשות לדרך עיר אחרת ובקשו בני אותן מבואות לסותמן בני אותה העיר מעכבים עליה אפילו יש להן דרך אחרת כו' וע"כ צ"ל הא דאמר בני אותו העיר לאו דוקא ואפילו מחילת כל אנשי העי לא מהני משום דכל בני העולם יכולים למחות וכ"מ שם סעיף א' ע"ש. ועיין בח"מ סי' תי"ז סעיף א' בהג' שכתב וז"ל וי"א אע"ג דהכי דינ' מ"מ כבר נהגו לעשות ביבין ומרתפות תחת חלל ר"ה כו' וכולן מוחלין על כך מאחר שכן נהגו:
ועוד שר"ה הם של מושלי העיר ולכל מה שנותנים רשות אזלינן בתריה ולפי ענין המנהג עכ"ל וע"ש בסמ"ע. וטעם השני שכתב רמ"א שם לענ"ד שייך גם לסכה:
ואת"ל דכל ישראל מוחלים משום דניח' לאינש למיעבד מצו' בממוניה בדבר שאין לו חסרון כיס גמור כדהכא. ועוד י"ל כמ"ש סמ"ע סימן תי"ז סעיף קטן ג'. וז"ל וכולן מוחלים על כך שהיום או מחר יצטרך גם הוא או בניו לעשות כן עכ"ל:
דוקא מישראל. אהא דאמר רב הונא שם לסוחרי לולב וכל הדברים הצריכים לו. כי קניתו הדסים מן הגוים במחובר יקצצן הגוי דסתם גוים גוזלי קרקעות הן. ושמא אות' קרקע גזול' היא וקרקע אינה נגזלת. ואין קונים ההדסים כ"א בשעת קציצ' דנעשו תלושים ונגזלים. לכן יקצץ הגוי ויהי' ייאוש ביד גוי ואחר כך שינוי רשות בידכם. ופירש"י סתם גוים גוזלי קרקעות הן גוזלי קרקע מישראל ושמא אות' קרקע מישראל הוי עכ"ל מלשון זה לכאור' משמע דאי גזלי מגוי מותר. וא"כ הי' מתיישב המנהג שעושים סכה בר"ה דהא ישראלים מוחלים ובגוים לא איכפת לן אפילו לא מחלי:
ואע"ג דקי"ל כו' בזה אתי לדחויי תי' זה. ובאמת לשון מ"א קצת מגומגם פה. והכוונ' דאין מרש"י ראי' להמנהג. דהא קי"ל גזל גוי אסור אלא דכוונת רש"י דבגוי ליכא משום מצו' הבא' בעביר'. וה"ט י"ל דרש"י לטעמי' דס"ל פ"ד דסנהדרין דגזל גוי אינו אסור אלא מדרבנן [וכמ"ש ש"ך בח"מ סי' שנ"ט ס"ק ב'] משום חילול השם. (ועיין באה"ע סי' כ"ח בב"ש ס"ק ה) קליש אסוריה ולא מיקרי מצו' הב"ע. ולפ"ז דבגוי ליכא משום מצו' הב"ע הוצרך לומר דגזלי מישראל כדי ליישב דברי רב הונא לכל שני הפירושים שכ' רש"י שם אהא דאמר ר"ה דליהוי יאוש ביד גוי ושינוי רשות בידכם וז"ל רש"י וקסבר יאוש גריד' לא קני אבל יאוש ושינוי רשות קני. ואי נמי קני מצו' הבא' בעביר' הוי עכ"ל ורצ' רש"י ליישב אפי' נאמר דרב הונא ס"ל ייאוש גרידא קני ואין האיסור כ"א משום מצו' הב"ע. וכיון דבגוי ליכא משום מהב"ע כנ"ל הוצרך לומר דגזלי מישראל וזה יספיק ליישב דברי רש"י אבל לא נתיישב מנהג העולם בזה דלדידן מלבד דדעת הרמב"ם גזל גוי אסור מן התור' וא"כ לדידיה גם בגוי יש משום מצו' הב"ע אלא אפ"ת דסמכו על דעת רש"י הנ"ל וליכא משום מהב"ע. מ"מ איכ' איסור גזל. וגם קי"ל ייאוש גרידא לא קני. וגם בלא"ה אע"ג דקרקע אינה נגזלת מ"מ לכתחל' אסור כמ"ש רמ"א בהג'. כיון דלא קניא. היינו משום דקרקע אינה נגזלת. ולכן לא הוי מצו' הב"ע כיון דלא נגמר' העביר':
כמ"ש ר"ס תרמ"ט דאם קנה לולב גזול או שאר ג' מינים בלי סיוע המצו' לא מיקרי מצו' הב"ע. ומ"מ לא יברך עליו דאין זה מברך אלא מנאץ. ודין ההוא נובע מדברי התוס' ריש פ"ג דסכה ובמקומות אחרים שהביא פה מ"א שכתב כאן היכי דקני דבר בלי סיוע המצו' ל"מ מצו' הב"ע. א"כ תיקשי הא דאמרי' במס' ב"ק גזל סאה חטין וטחנ' ואפא' אע"ג דשינוי קונה וקנאו בשינוי מעש' קודם הפרשת חלה אפ"ה אי מברך על הפרש' חלתה אין זה מברך אלא מנאץ. ואמאי הא כה"ג לא הוי מצו' הב"ע. ותי' לחד תירוצ' וז"ל שאני ברכ' דאיכ' נמי הזכר' לשם שמים עכ"ל:
machatzit_hashekel.en:
(Small paragraph 3) And so forth, for in the public domain, etc. See Choshen Mishpat siman 162, seif 2, where it says: likewise, alleyways open to the road of another city, if the people of those alleyways seek to close them, the people of that city may prevent them, even if they have another route, etc. Perforce, what it says "the people of that city" is not precise; even forgiveness by all the people of the city does not help, because all people in the world can protest. So too it appears there in seif 1; see there. See Choshen Mishpat siman 417, seif 1, in the gloss, where it says: Some say that although this is the law, nevertheless people have already practiced making drains and cellars under the open space of the public domain, etc., and everyone forgives this, since this is the custom.
Further, the public domains belong to the rulers of the city, and whatever they give permission for, we follow that, according to the nature of the custom. End quote. See there in the Sema. The second reason that the Rema wrote there, in my humble opinion, applies also to sukkah.
And if you say that all Jews forgive, because a person is pleased that a mitzvah be done with his property in a matter where there is no complete monetary loss, as here. Further, one can say as the Sema wrote in siman 417, small paragraph 3: "And everyone forgives this," because today or tomorrow he or his children will also need to do so. End quote.
Specifically from a Jew. This refers to what Rav Huna said there to the lulav merchants, and to all the items needed for it: when you buy myrtles from gentiles while attached, have the gentile cut them, for ordinary gentiles are robbers of land. Perhaps that land is stolen, and land is not stolen; the myrtles are acquired only at the time of cutting, when they become detached and subject to theft. Therefore the gentile should cut them, so that there is owner-despair in the gentile's hand and afterward a change of domain in your hand. Rashi explained: ordinary gentiles are robbers of land, meaning they rob land from Jews, and perhaps that land belonged to a Jew. End quote. From this language it seems at first glance that if they stole from a gentile it is permitted. If so, the custom of making a sukkah in the public domain would be resolved, for Jews forgive, and regarding gentiles we do not care even if they do not forgive.
And although we rule, etc. With this he comes to reject that answer. In truth, the language of the Magen Avraham is somewhat unclear here. The intent is that there is no proof from Rashi for the custom, because we rule that theft from a gentile is forbidden. Rather, Rashi's intent is that with a gentile there is no issue of a mitzvah that comes through a transgression. The reason may be that Rashi follows his own view in chapter 4 of Sanhedrin, that theft from a gentile is forbidden only rabbinically, as the Shach wrote in Choshen Mishpat siman 359, small paragraph 2, because of desecration of the Name. See Even HaEzer siman 28, Beit Shmuel small paragraph 5. Its prohibition is weak and is not called a mitzvah that comes through a transgression. According to this, since with a gentile there is no mitzvah that comes through a transgression, Rashi needed to say that they stole from a Jew in order to resolve Rav Huna's words according to both explanations Rashi wrote there regarding Rav Huna's statement that there should be owner-despair in the gentile's hand and change of domain in your hand. Rashi wrote: He holds that despair alone does not acquire, but despair and change of domain acquire. Alternatively, even if it does acquire, it is a mitzvah that comes through a transgression. End quote. Rashi wanted to resolve the matter even if we say Rav Huna holds despair alone acquires and the prohibition is only because of a mitzvah that comes through a transgression. Since with a gentile there is no mitzvah that comes through a transgression, as above, he needed to say that they stole from a Jew. This is enough to resolve Rashi's words, but the common custom is not resolved by this. For us, besides the fact that the Rambam's view is that theft from a gentile is Torah-forbidden, so according to him with a gentile too there is a mitzvah that comes through a transgression, even if you say they relied on Rashi's view above and there is no mitzvah that comes through a transgression, there is nevertheless a prohibition of theft. We also rule that despair alone does not acquire. Even aside from this, although land is not stolen, it is nevertheless forbidden at the outset, as the Rema wrote in the gloss, since it is not acquired; this is because land is not stolen. Therefore it is not a mitzvah that comes through a transgression, since the transgression was not completed.
As written at the beginning of siman 649: if one bought a stolen lulav or the other three species without the assistance of the mitzvah, it is not called a mitzvah that comes through a transgression. Nevertheless, one should not bless over it, for this is not blessing but blaspheming. That law derives from the words of Tosafot at the beginning of chapter 3 of Sukkah and in other places that the Magen Avraham brought here, who wrote here that where one acquired an item without the assistance of the mitzvah, it is not considered a mitzvah that comes through a transgression. If so, there is a difficulty from what we say in tractate Bava Kamma: one who stole a se'ah of wheat, ground it, and baked it, although change acquires and he acquired it through a physical change before separating challah, nevertheless if he blesses over separating its challah, this is not blessing but blaspheming. Why? In such a case it is not a mitzvah that comes through a transgression. Tosafot answered in one answer: blessing is different, because it also contains mention of the Name of Heaven. End quote.

magen_avraham.he:
גזולה כשרה. אינו מדוקדק דהא דרשינן לך למעוטי גזולה וכמש"ל אלא דבגזל קרקע כשרה דאינה נגזלת והוי ליה שאולה:
וכן בקרקע וכו'. וצריך עיון שנהגו קצת לעשות סוכ' ברשות הרבים ואם כן סוכה גזולה הוא וא"ל דבני העיר מוחלין להם דהא ברה"ר יש לכל העולם חלק בהם (עבח"מ סי' קס"ב ס"ב) ואת"ל דכל ישראל מוחלין מ"מ הרי יש לעכו"ם חלק בהם ומלשון רש"י בסוכה דף ל' ע"ב משמע דוקא מישראל אסור אבל מעכו"ם שרי ואף על גב דקי"ל גזל העכו"ם אסור מ"מ לא מקרי מצוה הבאה בעבירה וכ"כ הש"ג ורי"ו, אבל בס' יראים כתב דאפי' למ"ד גזל העכו"ם שרי מ"מ לא מקרי לכם ובתשו' הרשב"א סי' תתנ"ב כתב דמה שכ' רש"י מישראל ל"ד דהא גזל עכו"ם מעכו"ם אסור וישראל מעכו"ם נמי פסול וכ"כ ב"י ססי' תרס"ד וא"כ אסור לעשות סוכה בר"ה שהעכו"ם לא מחלי על כך (ועמ"ש סי' תר"מ ס"ב) ואף דבדיעבד כשרה מ"מ נ"ל דאין לברך עליה דאע"ג דלית בה משום מצוה הבאה בעביר' כיון דלא קניא כלל כמ"ש הר"ן ורי"ו מ"מ אין לברך עליה כמ"ש רסי' תרמ"ט וכ"מ בתוס' רפ"ג דסוכה וא"כ הוי ברכה לבטלה:
יצא. ומותר אח"כ לישב בה לכתחל' כדאי' בעובדא דריש גלותא:
דמי עצים. ואם אינו רוצה לתת דמי עצים לא יצא [טור ב"ה] וכן עיקר דהא מדאורייתא פסול בכל ענין כמ"ש הר"ן ותוס':
לא יצא. ערסי' תרמ"ט וגבי סוכה הוי כמו לולב בי"ט ראשון דכתיב לך למעוטי גזול':
לא יצא בה. דאין עלי' תורת שאולה כיון דלא קיימא ברשותו של ראובן ול"ד לקרקע דבחזקת הבעלים עומדת ולכך אין קרקע נגזלת עכ"ל התוס' ובהג"א כתב שלא מדעתו כ' הב"ח שכצ"ל בתוס' וכ"כ רש"א וכ"כ ד"מ אבל אם השאיל לו שמעון הקרקע לז' ימי החג ואח"כ הוציאו מסוכתו קיימי העצים ברשות ראובן ואינה נגזלת וה"ל כשאולה ביד שמעון (ב"ח) ומל' רמ"א שדילג תיבת שלא מדעתו משמע דס"ל דה"ה אם עשאה מדעת שמעון וכדאיתא בנוסחאות הישנים של התוס' דהא מ"מ אין הקרקע עומדת ברשות ראובן דאינה רק שאולה לז' ימים ואינה עומדת בחזקת ראובן וקשה דהא אף על פי שאין הקרקע נגזלת מ"מ העצים נגזלים וא"כ כשהוציא חבירו מסוכתו היא פסולה דהא אין כאן תקנת השבים כיון דלא טרח בה וצ"ל דמחובר לקרקע כקרקע, וקשה למ"ד בח"מ סי' צ"ה דבית לאו כמחובר לקרקע הוא ע"ש בהגה ועיין בש"ך שם שהרבה להשיב עליו וכל קושיותיו יש לדחות די"ל כיון דהקרקע נקנית בכסף בשטר ובחזקה נקנה הבית עמו דמטלטלים נקנה אגב קרקע וה"ה לאינך ע"ש כי אין כאן מקומו אך מכאן הוא קשה וי"ל כיון שלא קנה הקרקע גם העצים לא קנה דהא לא משך בהם וכ"כ בהדיא בב"ק סוף דף קי"ז דלרבנן דקרקע אינה נגזלת אפי' מטלטלין המונחים בתוכה אין נגזלים ולר"א הקרקע נגזלת והמטלטלין נקנין עם הקרקע ומעתה י"ל דלהכי נקט הג"א שלא מדעתו דאלו בנה מדעתו ה"ל הקרקע של ראובן וקרקע אינה נגזלת וא"כ לא קנה ג"כ העצים אך כיון שבנה שלא מדעתו א"כ שמעון גזל העצים בלבד דהוי מטלטלין ואפשר לסתור כסתור דמי עיין בח"מ צ"ה גבי כל העומד לגדור וא"כ ה"ל גזילה ותקנת השבים אין כאן כיון דלא טרח בה ומיהו בח"מ סי' שי"ג דכשהקרקע שאולה לאחרים קונה המטלטלין שעליה ועבי"ד סי' רכ"א ס"ז:

A stolen one is valid. This is not precise, for we expound "yours" to exclude a stolen one, as I wrote above. Rather, with stolen land it is valid, because land is not stolen and it is considered borrowed.
And likewise on land, etc. This requires examination, for some are accustomed to make a sukkah in the public domain. If so, it is a stolen sukkah. One cannot say that the people of the city forgive them, for everyone in the world has a share in the public domain (see Choshen Mishpat siman 162, seif 2). And even if you say that all Jews forgive, nevertheless gentiles also have a share in it. From Rashi's language in Sukkah 30b it implies that it is forbidden specifically from a Jew, but from a gentile it is permitted. Although we rule that theft from a gentile is forbidden, nevertheless it is not called a mitzvah that comes through a transgression; so wrote Shiltei HaGibborim and Rabbenu Yerucham. But in Sefer Yere'im he wrote that even according to the one who says theft from a gentile is permitted, nevertheless it is not called "yours." In Responsa Rashba, siman 852, he wrote that Rashi's wording "from a Jew" is not specific, for theft by a gentile from a gentile is forbidden, and a Jew who steals from a gentile is also invalid. So too wrote the Beit Yosef at the end of siman 664. If so, it is forbidden to make a sukkah in the public domain, for gentiles do not forgive this. See what I wrote in siman 640, seif 2. Although after the fact it is valid, nevertheless it seems to me that one should not recite a blessing over it. Even though it does not involve a mitzvah that comes through a transgression, since it is not acquired at all, as the Ran and Rabbenu Yerucham wrote, nevertheless one should not bless over it, as written at the beginning of siman 649, and so it appears from Tosafot at the beginning of chapter 3 of Sukkah. If so, it would be a blessing in vain.
He has fulfilled. Afterward it is permitted to sit in it at the outset, as stated in the incident of the Exilarch.
The value of the wood. If he does not want to give the value of the wood, he has not fulfilled [Tur, Ba'al HaItur]. This is primary, for by Torah law it is invalid in every case, as the Ran and Tosafot wrote.
He has not fulfilled. See the beginning of siman 649. Regarding sukkah it is like lulav on the first day of Yom Tov, for it is written "for yourself," to exclude a stolen one.
He has not fulfilled with it. For it does not have the status of a borrowed sukkah, since it does not stand in Reuven's domain. This is not like land, which remains in the possession of its owners, and therefore land is not stolen. End quote of Tosafot. In Hagahot Ashiri it says "without his knowledge"; the Bach wrote that this is how it should read in Tosafot, and so wrote R. Shmuel Eidels, and so wrote the Darchei Moshe. But if Shimon lent him the land for the seven days of the festival and afterward removed him from his sukkah, the wood stands in Reuven's domain and is not stolen, and it is like a borrowed sukkah in Shimon's hand (Bach). From the language of the Rema, who omitted the words "without his knowledge," it implies that he holds the same applies even if he made it with Shimon's knowledge, as is found in the old texts of Tosafot, for in any case the land does not stand in Reuven's domain; it is only borrowed for seven days and does not stand in Reuven's possession. This is difficult, for although land is not stolen, the wood is stolen; if so, when his fellow removes him from his sukkah it is invalid, since the enactment for repentant thieves does not apply because he did not toil in it. One must say that what is attached to the ground is like the ground. This is difficult according to the view in Choshen Mishpat siman 95 that a house is not like something attached to the ground; see there in the gloss, and see the Shach there, who answered him at length. All his questions can be rejected, for one can say that since land is acquired by money, document, and possession, the house is acquired with it, for movable items are acquired incidentally to land; and the same applies to the other matters; see there, for this is not the place. But from here it is difficult. One can say that since he did not acquire the land, he also did not acquire the wood, for he did not pull it. So it is explicit in Bava Kamma at the end of 117, that according to the rabbis who hold land is not stolen, even movable items lying within it are not stolen; and according to R. Eliezer, the land is stolen and the movable items are acquired together with the land. Now one can say that this is why Hagahot Ashiri specified "without his knowledge": if he built with his knowledge, the land is Reuven's, and land is not stolen, so he also did not acquire the wood. But since he built without his knowledge, Shimon stole only the wood, which is movable property; and what can be dismantled is considered as if already dismantled. See Choshen Mishpat 95 regarding anything standing to be cut down. If so, it is theft, and the enactment for repentant thieves does not apply, since he did not toil in it. However, in Choshen Mishpat siman 313, when land is lent to others, it acquires the movable items upon it. See Yoreh De'ah siman 221, seif 7.

mishnah_berurah.he:
(ז) סוכה גזולה כשרה - אין הלשון מדוקדק כ"כ דהא דרשינן מדכתיב חג הסוכות תעשה לך למעוטי גזולה אלא ר"ל דגזולה כהאי שתקף על חבירו והוציאו וכו' כשרה:
(ח) שאין הקרקע נגזלת - דכל המחובר לקרקע הרי הוא כקרקע והרי היא בחזקת בעליה הראשונים וכשאולה דמיא לדידיה:
(ט) שלא מדעתו - שמא בעל הסוכה הוא מקפיד ע"ז שלא יראה חבירו את עסקיו ואת אכילתו בלי ידיעתו וממילא אין נכון לברך עליה אבל מותר ליכנס ולישב בסוכת חבירו בשעה שאין בעל הסוכה שם בסוכתו שבודאי לא יקפיד ע"ז דניחא ליה לאינש דליעבד מצוה בממוניה ומ"מ אם אפשר שיבוא בעל הסוכה בעוד שהוא שם אף דבעת הכניסה אינו שם לא יכנס שלא מדעתו כי אפשר שבעה"ב יתבייש ליכנס ולאכול או לעשות עסק אחר בפניו. כתב בבכורי יעקב דאם נטל רשות מאשתו של חבירו כשאינו בביתו נראה דמהני דכיון דהרשתיה אשתו מסתמא לא יקפיד ע"ז:
(י) שהיא של רבים - כתב המ"א וצ"ע שנהגו קצת לעשות סוכה בר"ה ואת"ל דכל ישראל מוחלין מ"מ יש לעכו"ם חלק בהם והעלה דאסור מטעם זה לעשות סוכה בר"ה דעכו"ם בודאי לא מחלי ואף דבדיעבד כשרה מ"מ לא יברך עליה דהוי ברכה לבטלה ובא"ר כתב דברכה לבטלה לא הוי ע"ש שהאריך בזה וע"כ אם אין לו אחרת מותר לברך עליה וכן מצדד בספר מאמר מרדכי להקל ובתשובת שואל ומשיב סימן קכ"ח דרחוב שלפני הבית הם שלו ולא מקרי ר"ה ובפרט היכי שיש להם דעקאמענט משר העיר שיש להם רשות לעשות עירובין וסוכות אין לפקפק בזה [פ"ת] ועיין בבה"ל:
(יא) לא יקצצו - מיער של עכו"ם אפילו מדעת העכו"ם וטעם דין זה ופרטיו יתבאר לקמן בסימן תרמ"ט ס"א בהג"ה. ובמקום שיש רשות לאנשי המקום ליקח עצים מן היער בדינא דמלכותא אין איסור אם לוקח משם לסכך:
(יב) אלא יקנו אותם מעובדי כוכבים וכו' - והיינו שעכו"ם בעצמו יקצץ אותם מתחלה ואם העכו"ם גנב העצים מן היער עיין בבה"ל. וכתבו האחרונים דה"ה אם קצץ הישראל ונותן לחבירו ג"כ שרי דהוי יאוש ביד הראשון הקוצץ ושינוי רשות ביד השני:
(יג) דכל גזל וכו' - ר"ל דשמא גזל העכו"ם הקרקע ומ"מ אם א"א מותר לקצוץ בעצמו ובלבד שיטול רשות מבעל הקרקע ואפילו הוא עכו"ם:
(יד) אין עושין וכו' - ואין לברך לישב בסוכה ומ"מ לענין דין הקודם בסקי"ג במקום שאי אפשר שמותר לקצוץ בעצמו אפשר שמותר לברך במדינותינו שרוב הקרקעות שיש להעכו"ם ניתן להם מדין המלכות ודינא דמלכותא דינא ועיין לקמן בסימן תרס"ד בט"ז והעתקתי דבריו פה בבה"ל:
(טו) יצא שתקנת - כצ"ל. ר"ל אף דמדאורייתא פסולה היא אפילו אם ירצה לשלם עבור העצים דצריך לסתור הבנין ולהשיב הגזילה לבעליו מכל מקום כבר תקנו חכמים כדי שירצו בנ"א לעשות תשובה שאינו משלם לו אלא דמי עצים ודיו ויש כח בידם לעשות זה שהפקר ב"ד הפקר א"כ ממילא אם ישלם לו דמי עצים הוי אח"כ שלו ממש ומותר לישב בה וגם לברך עליה:
(טז) דמי עצים - ואם אינו רוצה לתת דמי עצים לא יצא:
(יז) אבל אם גזל סוכה וכו' - דאז היא עצמה נגזלת שאיננה מחובר לקרקע ואין עליו להחזיר דמים אלא כמות שהיא בנויה דאין כאן תקנת השבים שהרי לא טרח עליה לבנותה ולא הוציא עליה הוצאות הלכך גזולה היא:
(יח) לא יצא - דכתיב חג הסוכות תעשה לך שבעת ימים למעוטי גזולה דלא הוי לך ומשמע מדברי המ"א דאף אחרים שישבו בה ג"כ לא יצאו י"ח דלא הוי לך ולענ"ד צ"ע בזה ועיין בה"ל:
(יט) לא יצא בה - ולא דמיא להנ"ל בס"ב דהתם הקרקע בחזקת בעליה עומדת ואינה נגזלת וכל המחובר לקרקע הרי היא כקרקע משא"כ הכא לא קיימא הסוכה בקרקע דראובן א"כ לא גזל אלא העצים ולא הקרקע והוי גזולה:

(7) A stolen sukkah is valid - The wording is not entirely precise, for we derive from the verse "you shall make for yourself the festival of Sukkot" that a stolen sukkah is excluded. Rather, it means that a stolen sukkah of this sort, where one overpowered another and removed him, etc., is valid.
(8) For land is not stolen - Anything attached to the ground has the status of ground, and it remains in the possession of its original owners; for him it is like a borrowed sukkah.
(9) Without his knowledge - Perhaps the owner of the sukkah objects to this, because he does not want his fellow to see his affairs and his eating without his knowledge, and therefore it is not proper to recite a blessing over it. But it is permitted to enter and sit in another person's sukkah when the owner is not there in his sukkah, for he certainly does not object, since a person is pleased that a mitzvah be performed with his property. Nevertheless, if the owner of the sukkah may come while he is there, even though he was not there at the time of entry, he should not enter without his knowledge, for perhaps the owner will be embarrassed to enter and eat or do some other matter in his presence. Bikkurei Yaakov wrote that if one received permission from his fellow's wife when he is not home, it appears effective, for since his wife permitted it he presumably will not object.
(10) That belongs to the public - The Magen Avraham wrote that it requires study that some have the custom to make a sukkah in a public domain. Even if you say that all Israel waive their rights, non-Jews nevertheless have a share in it. He concludes that for this reason it is forbidden to make a sukkah in the public domain, since non-Jews certainly do not waive their rights. Although after the fact it is valid, one should not recite a blessing over it, for it would be a berachah levatalah. Eliyah Rabbah wrote that it is not a berachah levatalah; see there, where he discusses this at length. Therefore, if one has no other sukkah, he may bless over it. Maamar Mordechai likewise inclines to be lenient. In Responsa Shoel Umeishiv, siman 128, he writes that the street before the house belongs to them and is not called a public domain, especially where they have a document from the city officer granting permission to make eruvin and sukkot; there is no concern in this, as Pitchei Teshuvah writes. See Biur Halacha.
(11) They should not cut - From a non-Jew's forest, even with the non-Jew's consent. The reason for this law and its details will be explained below in siman 649 seif 1 in the gloss. In a place where the local people have permission to take wood from the forest by the law of the kingdom, there is no prohibition if one takes from there for sechach.
(12) Rather, they should buy them from non-Jews, etc. - Meaning that the non-Jew himself should cut them at first. If the non-Jew stole the wood from the forest, see Biur Halacha. The later authorities wrote that the same applies if a Jew cut it and gives it to his fellow: it is also permitted, for there was despair in the hand of the first cutter and a change of domain in the hand of the second.
(13) For every theft, etc. - Meaning, perhaps the non-Jew stole the land. Nevertheless, if it is impossible, one may cut it himself, provided that he takes permission from the owner of the land, even if he is a non-Jew.
(14) One does not make, etc. - And one should not recite the blessing "to sit in the sukkah." Nevertheless, regarding the preceding law in seif katan 13, where in a case of impossibility it is permitted to cut it himself, perhaps one may bless in our countries, for most of the lands that non-Jews have were given to them by the law of the kingdom, and dina demalchuta dina. See below in siman 664 in the Taz; I copied his words here in Biur Halacha.
(15) The enactment resulted - So it should read. Meaning, although by Torah law it is invalid even if he wants to pay for the wood, because he must dismantle the structure and return the stolen item to its owners, nevertheless the Sages already enacted, so that people would be willing to repent, that he pays only the value of the wood and that suffices. They have the authority to do this, for hefker beit din hefker. Consequently, if he pays the value of the wood, it afterwards becomes truly his, and it is permitted to sit in it and also to bless over it.
(16) The value of the wood - If he does not want to give the value of the wood, he has not fulfilled.
(17) But if he stole a sukkah, etc. - Then the sukkah itself is stolen, since it is not attached to the ground, and he is not obligated to return money but the structure as it is built. There is no enactment for penitents here, for he did not toil over it to build it and did not spend expenses on it; therefore it is stolen.
(18) He has not fulfilled - For it is written, "you shall make for yourself the festival of Sukkot for seven days," excluding a stolen sukkah, which is not "yours." From the words of the Magen Avraham it implies that others who sat in it also did not fulfill their obligation, for it is not "yours"; in my humble opinion this requires study. See Biur Halacha.
(19) He has not fulfilled with it - This is not comparable to what was said above in seif 2, for there the land remains in the possession of its owner and is not stolen, and anything attached to the ground has the status of ground. Here, however, the sukkah does not stand on Reuven's land, so he stole only the wood and not the land, and it is stolen.

turei_zahav.he:
וכן לא יקצצו ישראל כו'. נ"ל במקום שיש רשות לאנשי המקום ליקח עצי' מן היער בדינא דמלכותא אין איסור אם לוקח הישראל שם לסכך ודומה למאי דאי' בפ' הגוזל בתרא דקטלינן דיקלא ועבדי' מהן גשורי ועברינן עלייהו ועמ"ש סי' תרס"ד מזה:
אבל אם גזל סוכם כו'. דאז היא עצמה נגזלת שאין מחוברת לקרקע ואין עליו להחזיר דמים אלא כמו שהיא בנוי' דאין כאן תקנת השבים שהרי לא טרח עליה לבנותה ולא הוציא עליה הוצאות הלכך גזולה היא (רש"י) נ"ל פשוט שמותר לאדם ליכנס לסוכתו של חבירו שלא מדעתו דניחא ליה לאינש דליעבד מצו' בממונו והוא ק"ו ממה דאיתא בסי' תרמ"ט דמותר לו לאדם ליטול לולב של חבירו שלא מדעתו דודאי קפיד אדם טפי על האתרוג ולולב ממה שקפיד על כניס' לסוכה שלו אלא דנ"ל דהיינו כ"ז שבעל סוכ' אינו שם אבל בשעה שהוא שם אפשר דקפיד עליו שלא יראה חבירו עסקיו ואכילתו בלי ידיעתו וזה דבר מוסכם מצד הסברא כנ"ל:
turei_zahav.en:
And likewise Jews should not cut, etc. It seems to me that in a place where the people of the place have permission to take wood from the forest by the law of the kingdom, there is no prohibition if the Jew takes from there for roofing. It resembles what is stated in the final chapter of HaGozel, that they cut palm trees, made bridges from them, and crossed over them. See what I wrote in siman 664 about this.
But if he stole a sukkah, etc. For then it itself is stolen, since it is not attached to the ground. He is not obligated to return money, but to return it as it is built, for the enactment for repentant thieves does not apply here, since he did not toil to build it and did not spend expenses on it; therefore it is stolen (Rashi). It seems obvious to me that it is permitted for a person to enter his fellow's sukkah without his knowledge, for a person is pleased that a mitzvah be done with his property. This is a fortiori from what is stated in siman 649, that it is permitted for a person to take his fellow's lulav without his knowledge, for a person is certainly more particular about his etrog and lulav than about someone entering his sukkah. However, it seems to me that this applies only as long as the owner of the sukkah is not there. But when he is there, perhaps he objects, lest his fellow see his affairs and eating without his knowledge. This is agreed by reasoning, as appears to me.

yad_ephraim.he: במג"א ס"ק ז' אבל אם השאיל לו שמעון הקרקע כו' נראה דס"ל דאם חיבר עצים שלו לקרקע חבירו אין דינו כמחובר לקרקע ושפיר הם נגזלים. משום דדוקא לקרקע שלו ומחובר לקרקע הרי הוא כקרקע ולכן אם השאיל לו הקרקע לז' ימים ס"ל דהוה כמחובר לקרקע שלו כיון שמדעתו חובר ולכן גם העצים אינם נגזלים אבל הד"מ שדלג תיבת שלא מדעתו ס"ל דגם מדעתו לא מהני כל שאין הקרקע שלו ממש רק על דרך שאולה לז' ימים ואח"כ הדרא ארעא למריה ויכול לומר טול עצים ואבניך ובכה"ג אין דינם כקרקע לכן גם מדעתו שפיר העצים נגזלים. ומ"ש המג"א וקשה כו' נראה שר"ל דקשה על הד"מ שדולג תיבת שלא מדעתו משום דמשמע ליה לחלק כנ"ל דבאמת ז"א דהא צריך להבין בגוף הדין דתוקף על חבירו כו' דהא העצים נגזלים כו' וע"כ לומר משום דלא משך וע"כ לחנם השמיט הד"מ תיבת שלא מדעתו דשפיר נקט המג"א שלא מדעתו דאז שפיר קנה שמעון עצים בגזילה אג"ק שלו וכיון דהעצים גזולין לא יצא משא"כ כשבונה מדעתו שהקרקע שאולה ביד ראובן ומה שגזל שמעון לא מהני דאין קרקע נגזלת ואם כן לא קנה שמעון העצים וע"ז כתב דבח"מ משמע שהמשאיל קונה אג"ק אעפ"י שהיא שאולה ביד אחרים כך הוא כוונת המג"א. אך לולי דברי אא"ז מהרש"א ז"ל והב"ח הייתי אומר דנהפוך היא וט"ס נפל בהג"ה וצ"ל מדעתו כמו בתוס' משום דהא שהשאיל הקרקע לראובן אם חוזר ותקפה והחזיק בה לעצמו נלענ"ד דמהני ולא שייך בזה קרקע אינה נגזלת דהא הטעם משום דשם בעלים עליו וכיון דאינו רק בתורת שאלה והוא חוזר וגוזל מה ששאל ממנו לא שייך שם בעלים ושפיר נגזלת והלכך לא יצא מחמת גזילת הקרקע משא"כ שלא מדעתו שלא גזל הקרקע כלל ומחמת גזל עצים לא מיירי כלל דמחמת זה אל"מ דיצא משום תקנת השבים אך בד"מ מסיים בלשון הג"א משום גזל העצים ובאמת בהג"ה גופיה לא מסיים בה כמ"ש בד"מ נראה דהכל א"ש דהג"ה העתיק לשון התוספת שכתבו על רש"י בחנם דחק כו' והיינו לומר דאפילו נאמר דשייך תקנת השבים אפילו היכא דלא טרח בה מכל מקום משכחת לה שפיר כשבנה מדעתו ואיכא גזל קרקע כמו שכתבתי לעיל. והד"מ העתיק הדין לדידן דקי"ל דהיכא דלא טרח לא שייך תקנת השבים ולכך השמיט תיבת מדעתו דאפילו שלא מדעתו אינו יוצא משום גזל דעצים כנלענ"ד:
yad_ephraim.en: In the Maga Sec. 7, but if Shimon lent him the land, etc., it appears that DSL Dam connected his trees to his friend's land, it is not his law as connected to the land, and Shafir, they are stolen. Because he is directly connected to his land and connected to the land, he is like land, therefore if he lent him the land to G. Yamim, S.L. Deva as connected to his land, since his mind is connected, therefore the trees are not stolen, but the DM who skipped a box without his knowledge Sal Model, in his opinion, does not have any real land, only on a road borrowed for 7 days, and after that, the Haara will graze Marya, and he can say that your trees and stones, and in the 23rd, have no right to them as land, therefore, in his opinion, the trees are stolen. It seems that Ral Daksha on the DM who skipped a box without his knowledge because he meant to divide as above Dabamat ZA Daha should be understood in the body of the law firmly on his friend 20 Daha the trees are robbed 20 and so on to say because he did not pull and ak Lahanm he left the DM a box without his knowledge Dashpir took the Maja without his knowledge then Shafir bought Shimon trees by robbery His AGC, and since the trees were cut off, there was no MGA when the builder thought that the land borrowed from Reuven's hand, and what Shimon stole from Reuven, is not a right to usurped land, and if so, Shimon did not buy the trees, and the OT wrote the DBM, meaning that the lender buys a OT, which is borrowed from others, that is the intention of the MGA. And Ts fell out of his mind in Haga and Tzal as in Tos because he lent the land to Reuven if he returns and it is valid and he kept it for himself, it is a presumption that he does not belong to it, the land is not usurped because the owner owns it and since we are only entitled to it in the Torah of a question and he comes back and usurps what he borrowed does not belong to an owner and Shafir is usurped and this is not because of the usurpation of the land, but it is not in his mind that he did not usurp the land at all and because of usurpation Trees are not set on fire at all, because of the regulation of the returnees, but in the DM, it ends with the language of the GA, because of the plundering of the trees, and in truth, in the Hagai, Gofia does not end with it as a mash in the DM. From his own mind, he stole land, as I wrote above, and the DM who passed the law on this matter does not belong to the statute of returnees, and therefore he omitted a box from his own mind.
